items.title: Jon Hendricks interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 29, 2000 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: So I went up and they were doing “The Song Is You.” ... So that I scatted. I scatted about ten choruses. ... And after the set he came over to my table, sat down, talked to me ... I had no trouble making entree into the jazz scene. ... And that’s how I got my start in New York.

ctx.x: We had this quick bandstand conversation. I had all his records when I came out of the Army. I had heard “Salt Peanuts” on the ship. I had won $300 shooting craps on the boat, and I heard this record from the ship’s radio room [scats]. I said whoa. Because it was in my head already from my Art Tatum days. And you know I heard Art Tatum, so I ran up to the radio room and I said to the guy, “what’s that record you just played?” Because by that time he’s playing something else. He said, “I don’t know it’s down there…
Forget it, man, I’ve got 25 bucks.

items.title: Jon Hendricks — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: He’s playing The Song is You. So I walked past the bandstand ... 'Hey, Jon. How you doing, man? You want to sing some?'

ctx.x: Yes. That’s okay. Now, tell us about your rendezvous with Charlie Parker.

First let me sum up that idea with Parker with Art Tatum. What Bird did when he got back to Kansas City was do exactly what he said. First thing he did was, he realized, hearing Art play, that he didn’t know the tunes that he was playing, because he was playing them only in one key. He realized that if he was to be said to know any song, he would have to know how to play it in any key. So he started by going back over his whole repertoire and playing it in all the keys and playing it accurately in every key. If…

Let’s say for you, you probably can do that, but just in terms of your range, whether or not you can actually hit all of the notes in a particular key – sometimes you can. Sometimes you can’t. But you would know the song conceptually.

items.title: Jon Hendricks — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: The chords are altered according to Tatumesque things and Bird and Diz’s contributions, but it’s the same source.

ctx.x: What – in 1953 and 1954, what was the relationship between jazz and rhythm-and-blues during that period.

Very close. One evolved out of the other. Jazz was nothing but a more sophisticated rhythm-and-blues. It’s like the city mouse and the country mouse. The country mouse comes to visit the city mouse, and he lives in a penthouse rather than on a farm. Rhythm-and-blues is like the country version of what the jazz people played. The blues are played a little faster. The chords are altered according to Tatumesque things and Bird and Diz’s contributions, but it’s the same source. The source is the same: the spirituals.…
